t.3.61.1: Having slain the hunter, the lotus-eyed one set out into the forest, terrifying and desolate, resounding with swarms of crickets.
t.3.61.2: It was haunted by lions, tigers, boars, bears, ruru deer and leopards, filled with flocks of many kinds of birds, and frequented by barbarians and thieves.
t.3.61.3: It was a forest densely covered with śāla, bamboo, dhava, aśvattha, tinduka, iṅguda and kiṃśuka trees, with arjuna and ariṣṭa trees, and with sandalwood trees along with śālmali trees.
t.3.61.4: It was thick with jambu, mango, lodhra, khadira, teak and cane, and covered with kāśmarya, āmalaka, plakṣa, kadamba and udumbara trees.
t.3.61.5: It was thickly covered with jujube and bilva trees and crowded with banyans, and with priyāla, palmyra, date-palm, harītaka and vibhītaka trees.
t.3.61.6: She saw various mountains studded with hundreds of different minerals, thickets resounding with the cries of birds, and caves wondrous to behold, rivers, lakes and ponds, and many kinds of beasts and birds.
t.3.61.7: She saw many Piśācas, serpents and Rākṣasas of fearsome form, and everywhere pools, ponds and mountain peaks, rivers and oceans, wondrous to behold.
t.3.61.8: And there the daughter of the lord of Vidarbha saw, in herds, buffaloes, boars, jackals, bears, monkeys and serpents.
t.3.61.9: Endowed with radiance, fame, steadfastness and supreme beauty, the princess of Vidarbha then wandered alone, searching for Nala.
t.3.61.10: Having reached that dreadful forest, the king's daughter Bhaimī, worn down by her husband's misfortune, then feared nothing there at all.
t.3.61.11: O king, the daughter of Vidarbha, deeply distressed, her limbs overwhelmed by grief for her husband, lamented as she rested upon the surface of a rock.
t.3.61.12: O lion-chested, mighty-armed lord of the Niṣadhas, where, O king, have you gone, abandoning me here in this desolate forest?
t.3.61.13: O hero, having offered the Aśvamedha and other sacrifices with ample fees, how is it, O tiger among men, that you behave falsely toward me?
t.3.61.14: What you said in my presence, O tiger among men, O greatly splendid one, you ought to make true, O noble one, O bull among kings.
t.3.61.15: O lord of the earth, you ought to consider what the birds, the swans, said in your presence and what they said in mine.
t.3.61.16: On one side stand the four Vedas, with their limbs and subsidiary limbs and in all their fullness, thoroughly studied, O best of men; on the other side, they say, stands truth alone.
t.3.61.17: Therefore, O slayer of foes, O lord of men, you ought to make true the words that you once spoke, O hero, in my presence.
t.3.61.18: Alas, O hero, O sinless one, surely I am, as they say, dear to you! Why then do you not answer me in this dreadful forest?
t.3.61.19: This fierce king of the forest, with gaping mouth and dreadful form, possessed by hunger, threatens me. Why do you not rescue me?
t.3.61.20: "O fortunate lady, no other woman is dear to me but you," you said then. O auspicious king, make true those words you spoke before.
t.3.61.21: O lord of men, why do you not answer me, your beloved wife, frantic and lamenting? O master, you who are longed for, why do you not speak to me, who long for you?
t.3.61.22: O lord of the earth, they saw her emaciated, wretched, pale and soiled, covered with half a garment, alone, lamenting like one who has no protector.
t.3.61.23: O wide-eyed one, worthy of honor, tormentor of foes, you do not heed me, weeping all alone like a doe strayed from her herd.
t.3.61.24: O great king, here in the great forest I, your own wife, a virtuous woman all alone, am calling out to you; why do you not answer me?
t.3.61.25: O best of men, you who are endowed with noble lineage and good character, splendid in all your lovely limbs, today I do not see you on this mountain, nor in this exceedingly dreadful forest frequented by lions and tigers.
t.3.61.26: Whether lying down or seated, standing or setting forth, O lord of the Niṣadhas, O best of men, may I behold you, you who heighten my grief!
t.3.61.28: Who, pray, would tell me today of Nala, dwelling in this forest, the handsome, great-souled destroyer of the enemy's battle-arrays?
t.3.61.27: Whom shall I ask, I who am stricken with sorrow and worn thin by grief on your account? Have you, meeting him here in the forest, seen King Nala?
t.3.61.30: This tiger, the glorious king of the forest, with four great fangs and mighty jaws, is coming straight toward me; I shall question him without fear.
t.3.61.29: From whom shall I hear today the sweet words, “This is he, King Nala with eyes like lotuses, whom you are seeking”?
t.3.61.31: You, sir, are the lord of the beasts; you are the master in this forest. Know me to be Damayantī, the daughter of the king of Vidarbha.
t.3.61.32: O king of beasts, if you have seen Nala here, console me, the wife of Nala, lord of the Niṣadhas and slayer of his foes, who wanders alone in search of her husband, wretched and worn down by grief.
t.3.61.33: Or else, O king of the forest, if you will not tell me of Nala, then devour me, O best of beasts, and free me, sorrowful as I am, from my grief.
t.3.61.34: Having heard my lament in the forest, this king of beasts himself goes away toward this river of pure water that flows to the sea.
t.3.61.36: Strewn with many kinds of minerals and adorned with various stones, it rises high like a banner of this great forest.
t.3.61.35: This holy mountain, with its many towering peaks, radiant and touching the sky, many-hued and delightful to the mind.
t.3.61.38: This king of mountains, adorned with kiṃśuka, aśoka, bakula and puṃnāga trees, adorned too with rivers full of birds and with lofty peaks, I shall now ask about the king.
t.3.61.37: It was teeming with lions, tigers, elephants, boars, bears and deer, and resounded on every side with the calls of birds of many kinds.
t.3.61.40: Having approached you, I bow to you. Know me to be a king's daughter, a king's daughter-in-law, a king's wife, renowned as Damayantī.
t.3.61.39: O blessed one, best of mountains, of divine appearance and wide renown, giver of refuge, abounding in auspiciousness, homage be to you, O upholder of the earth!
t.3.61.41: My father is the king, lord of Vidarbha, a great chariot-warrior, a ruler of the earth named Bhīma, protector of the four varṇas.
t.3.61.42: He is the performer of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, rites rich in sacrificial fees, the best of kings, with large, lovely, curving eyes.
t.3.61.43: He is devoted to brahmins, of virtuous conduct, truthful in speech and free from envy; he is of good character and upright behavior, of great splendor, a knower of dharma, and pure.
t.3.61.44: The lord who rightly protects the Vidarbhas, by whom hosts of foes have been conquered: know me, O blessed one, to be his daughter, who has come before you.
t.3.61.45: O great mountain, among the Niṣadhas my father-in-law was the best of kings, a man of auspicious name, renowned as Vīrasena.
t.3.61.46: That king's son, a hero, glorious and of true valor, is the one who now rules his father's own kingdom, which has come to him by succession.
t.3.61.47: He is named Nala, the subduer of foes, renowned as Puṇyaśloka, devoted to brahmins, versed in the Vedas, eloquent, a doer of meritorious deeds, a drinker of soma, and a builder of the sacred fire altar.
t.3.61.48: He is a sacrificer, a giver of gifts, a warrior, and a righteous ruler; know me, O best of mountains, to be his wife, who has come here.
t.3.61.49: Me, bereft of fortune, deprived of my husband, without a protector, beset by misfortune, searching for my husband, that best of the best of men.
t.3.61.50: O best of mountains, with these hundreds of peaks of yours that scrape the sky, have you perhaps seen King Nala in this dreadful forest?
t.3.61.51: Have you perhaps seen Nala, lord of the Niṣadhas, my illustrious husband, who strides like a lordly elephant, wise, long-armed and intolerant of wrong, valiant, steadfast and truthful in speech?
t.3.61.52: O best of mountains, why do you not comfort me today with your words, as I lament alone in my sorrow, as you would comfort your own grieving daughter?
t.3.61.53: O hero, O valiant one, O knower of dharma, O you who are true to your word, O lord of the earth! If you are in this forest, O king, show yourself to me in your own person.
t.3.61.54: When, oh when, shall I hear that voice of the Naiṣadha, tender and deep, like the rumbling of a rain-cloud, a voice like nectar?
t.3.61.55: When shall I hear that auspicious voice of the great-souled king, calling out simply "Vaidarbhī!", a voice rich and true to the sacred tradition, which drives away my grief?
t.3.61.57: Having journeyed for three days and nights, that most excellent woman beheld an incomparable forest of ascetics, which had the appearance of a heavenly grove.
t.3.61.56: Having thus spoken to that best of mountains, Damayantī, the daughter of the king, then went on once more toward the northern direction.
t.3.61.58: It was adorned with ascetics equal to Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu and Atri, self-restrained men who curbed their food and were endowed with self-control and purity.
t.3.61.59: It was inhabited by illustrious ascetics who had conquered their senses, who lived on water alone, on air alone, and likewise on leaves, longing to behold the path to heaven.
t.3.61.60: She beheld a delightful circle of hermitages, inhabited by ascetics, by sages clad in bark and deerskin, with their senses restrained.
t.3.61.61: As soon as she saw the hermitage, frequented by many kinds of animals and filled with troops of monkeys and with ascetics,
t.3.61.63: She entered the hermitage grounds, the beloved of Vīrasena's son, a jewel among women, the illustrious and high-minded Damayantī.
t.3.61.62: She had lovely brows, beautiful hair, shapely hips, fair breasts and a face graced with fine teeth; she was radiant and firmly poised, and she moved with a graceful, stately gait.
t.3.61.64: Having saluted those rich in austerities, she stood bowed down in humility, and she was addressed by all those ascetics with the words, "Welcome to you!"
t.3.61.65: And having paid her due honor there, as was proper, those ascetics rich in austerity then said to her, "Be seated; tell us, what shall we do for you?"
t.3.61.66: The fair-hipped lady said to them: "I trust, O sinless ones, that all is well with you blessed ones here, in your austerities, your sacred fires, your religious duties, and with the beasts and birds, and also in the practice of your own dharma, O greatly fortunate ones?"
t.3.61.67: The illustrious lady was told by them, "All is well everywhere, gentle lady. Tell us, you whose every limb is flawless, who are you, and what do you wish to do?"
t.3.61.68: Merely on seeing that supreme beauty and supreme radiance here, wonder has arisen in us. Take heart, do not grieve.
t.3.61.69: Are you the great goddess of this forest, or of the mountain, or of this river, O fair one? Speak the truth, O blameless lady.
t.3.61.70: She said to those seers, "I am not the deity of this forest, nor of this mountain, O brahmins, nor am I the deity of the river."
t.3.61.71: Know me to be a human woman, all of you ascetics rich in austerity. I shall tell it at length; hear it from me in full.
t.3.61.72: Among the Vidarbhas there is a king named Bhīma, of great splendor; know me, all of you, O best of the twice-born, to be his daughter.
t.3.61.73: The wise lord of the Niṣadhas, named Nala, of great fame, a hero, victor in battle, learned, a lord of the people, is my husband.
t.3.61.74: Devoted to the worship of the gods and loving toward the twice-born, he is the protector of the Niṣadha lineage, greatly fortunate and of great splendor.
t.3.61.75: He is truthful in speech, a knower of dharma, wise, true to his promises, a crusher of foes, devoted to brahmins, intent on the gods, glorious, a conqueror of enemy cities.
t.3.61.76: My husband is the best of kings, Nala by name, equal in splendor to the king of the gods, large-eyed, with a face like the full moon, a slayer of foes.
t.3.61.77: He is a performer of the foremost sacrifices, one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, a slayer of his rivals in battle, with a radiance equal to that of the sun and the moon.
t.3.61.78: That protector of the earth, devoted to truth and dharma, was challenged by certain base and wicked men, wise in deceit, crooked and skilled at dicing, and was defeated, losing his kingdom and his wealth.
t.3.61.79: Know me to be the wife of that bull among kings, renowned as Damayantī, longing to behold my husband.
t.3.61.80: She passed through forests and mountains, lakes and rivers, lovely ponds, and wildernesses on every side.
t.3.61.81: Searching for my husband Nala, skilled in battle, great-souled and accomplished in weapons, I wander here in sorrow.
t.3.61.82: Has a king named Nala, lord of the Niṣadhas, perhaps come to this holy penance grove of you blessed ones?
t.3.61.83: O brahmins, it is on his account that I have entered this exceedingly cruel forest, frightful and terrible, frequented by tigers and wild beasts.
t.3.61.84: If within some days and nights I do not see King Nala, I shall unite myself with the highest good by releasing myself from this body.
t.3.61.85: What use indeed is life to me without that bull among men? How shall I exist today, tormented by grief for my husband?
t.3.61.86: Then those truth-speaking ascetics spoke to Damayantī, the daughter of Bhīma, as she lamented thus, alone in the forest.
t.3.61.87: Your future, O fair lady, will be auspicious, O lovely one. We see it through our austerity: soon you will see the Naiṣadha.
t.3.61.88: O Bhaimī, you will see Nala, lord of the Niṣadhas, slayer of foes, best of those who uphold dharma, freed from his fever of distress.
t.3.61.90: O fair lady, you will see your husband, the king of noble lineage, who brings fear to his enemies and dispels the sorrow of his friends.
t.3.61.89: You shall see that tamer of foes, freed from all sins and endowed with every jewel, ruling that very same best of cities.
t.3.61.91: Having spoken thus to the beloved chief queen of Nala, the king's daughter, those ascetics then vanished, together with their agnihotra fires and their hermitages.
t.3.61.92: Having seen that great wonder, she, Damayantī of flawless limbs, the daughter-in-law of King Vīrasena, was then filled with amazement.
t.3.61.93: Was it a dream that I saw? What strange happening has taken place here? Where now are all those ascetics, and where is that circle of hermitages?
t.3.61.94: Where is that lovely river of holy waters, frequented by many kinds of birds? And where are those charming trees, adorned with fruits and flowers?
t.3.61.95: Having brooded for a long time, Damayantī of the bright smile, daughter of Bhīma, wholly overcome by grief for her husband and miserable, became pale of face.
t.3.61.96: Then, having gone on to another region, she, her eyes filled with tears, saw an aśoka tree and lamented there in a voice choked with weeping.
t.3.61.97: Then, approaching an aśoka in full bloom, the finest of trees, crowned with tender shoots, delightful to the heart, and resounding with the calls of birds,
t.3.61.99: Quickly make me free of sorrow, O Aśoka, lovely to behold! Have you perhaps seen the king, free of sorrow, fear and affliction?
t.3.61.98: Ah, alas, you have come into the depths of this forest! This splendid one shines with its many garlands like the splendid king of the Dramiḍas.
t.3.61.100: Have you seen Nala by name, the tamer of foes, the beloved husband of Damayantī, the lord of the Niṣadhas, my beloved?
t.3.61.101: the hero clad in half of a single garment, his skin soft and delicate, who, afflicted by misfortune, has come to this forest.
t.3.61.102: O Aśoka tree, act so that I may go free from sorrow; O Aśoka, be true to your name by destroying my sorrow.
t.3.61.103: Thus, having circled that aśoka tree three times, she, the afflicted daughter of Bhīma, that most excellent of women, went on to a still more dreadful region.
t.3.61.104: She saw many trees, and likewise many rivers, many lovely mountains, and many beasts and birds.
t.3.61.105: Then the daughter of Bhīma, searching for her husband, beheld caves and mountain slopes and rivers wondrous to behold.
t.3.61.106: Having travelled a long way, Damayantī of the bright smile then saw a great caravan crowded with elephants, horses and chariots.
t.3.61.108: She saw a river resounding with the cries of krauñcas and ospreys, echoing with the calls of cakravākas, teeming with tortoises, crocodiles and fish, and adorned with sandbanks and islands.
t.3.61.107: …as it was crossing a lovely, auspicious river with clear, very cool water, a broad river full of deep pools and lined with reeds.
t.3.61.109: As soon as she saw the great caravan, Nala's glorious wife, the fair-hipped one, approached it and entered into the midst of the people.
t.3.61.110: Looking like a madwoman, stricken with grief, and covered with only half a garment, she was emaciated, pale and soiled, her hair begrimed with dust.
t.3.61.111: Seeing her there, some of the people fled in fear; some stood still, lost in anxious thought; and some there cried out aloud.
t.3.61.112: Some laughed at her, while others scorned her; some took pity on her and also questioned her, O Bhārata.
t.3.61.113: Who are you, and whose are you, lovely lady? Or what are you seeking in the forest? Seeing you, we are troubled here; are you perhaps a human woman?
t.3.61.114: Tell the truth: are you the goddess of this forest, of the mountain, or of the quarters? For you are a deity, O fair one, and we have come to you for refuge.
t.3.61.115: Whether you are a Yakṣī or a Rākṣasī, or else a most excellent woman, in every way bring us well-being; protect us, O blameless one.
t.3.61.117: Thus addressed by that caravan, Damayantī, the king's daughter, the virtuous woman grieving over her husband's misfortune, then replied to the caravan leader, to the caravan, and to whatever people were there.
t.3.61.116: O auspicious lady, arrange things so that this caravan may go swiftly from here, safe in every way. We have come to you for refuge.
t.3.61.118: O young men, old men and boys, and you leaders of the caravan, know me to be a human woman, the daughter of a lord of men, the daughter-in-law of a king, the wife of a king, longing to see my husband.
t.3.61.119: The king of Vidarbha is my father, and my husband is the king of the Niṣadhas, the illustrious one named Nala; it is him, the unconquered, whom I am searching for.
t.3.61.121: To her of faultless limbs spoke the lord of that great caravan, the caravan-leader named Śuci: "Listen, fair lady, to my words."
t.3.61.120: If you know of the king, my beloved Nala, that tiger among kings, slayer of hosts of enemies, tell me quickly.
t.3.61.122: I am indeed the leader of this caravan, its caravan-master, O sweetly smiling one; I do not see any man named Nala, O glorious lady.
t.3.61.123: I see elephants, leopards, buffaloes, tigers, bears and deer in this dreadful forest, which is frequented by beings other than humans. So may Maṇibhadra, king of the Yakṣas, be gracious to us today.
t.3.61.124: Then she spoke to all the merchants and to that leader of the caravan: "Where, pray, will you go, this caravan of yours? You ought to tell me this."
t.3.61.125: O daughter of man, this caravan will soon go to the country of Subāhu, the truthful king of the Cedis, for the sake of profit.
